steps.title: Setting up DigiD
steps.body: Install the DigiD app, link face recognition or a fingerprint, and you're set. You'll use it for DUO (student finance!), the Tax Office, your health insurer, and MijnOverheid, among others.

steps.title: Message box: never miss a DUO or tax deadline
steps.body: Go to MijnOverheid > Message box and turn on an email reminder. This way you won't miss a message from DUO about your student debt or funding, without having to actively check the site.

steps.title: DigiD is personal — not even 'just quickly' for a housemate
steps.body: Never share your DigiD details with anyone — not even 'just quickly' for a housemate who lost their own. The government will never call or message you asking for a DigiD code.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Browse MijnOverheid below and check whether your message box reminders are turned on.

steps.title: Crypto and 'finfluencer' scams
steps.body: A TikTok or Instagram account promises quick riches with crypto or stocks, sometimes using a fake video of a well-known influencer or celebrity. Almost always fake. Never invest via a link from an ad or DM; always go to a recognized, regulated provider (check its official registration).

steps.title: A 'side gig' that's actually money laundering (money mule)
steps.body: An offer to 'simply' receive money in your account and forward it for a small commission is money laundering — even if you don't think of it that way. You end up in criminal trouble yourself, and your bank account can get frozen. Never agree to this, no matter how tempting the offer sounds.

steps.title: Ticket and 'too-good-to-be-true' scams
steps.body: A festival ticket, concert seat, or console that's sold out everywhere, yet somehow 'just' available via a DM or unknown site — assume it's a scam. Only buy through official sellers or platforms with buyer protection (like verified resale on Ticketswap).

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Check your banking app and see whether you get notified of unusual transactions.

steps.title: Phishing is getting more personal
steps.body: Classic phishing is generic ('Dear customer'). Spear-phishing targets you specifically: a DM from a 'friend' whose account got hacked, a fake recruiter on LinkedIn, or a fake delivery notice that knows you recently bought something on Vinted or Marktplaats.

steps.title: Exercise: an inbox full of fake emails
steps.body:
Below is an inbox with six recreated example emails — some are phishing, some are simply safe. Open each one, read it carefully, and choose at the bottom whether you think it’s safe or suspicious.

From: PostNL <delivery@postnl-track-parcel.info>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Delivery failed: reschedule within 24 hours

Dear customer,

Unfortunately we were unable to deliver your parcel. There is an outstanding amount of €0.49 in shipping costs. Pay this within 24 hours or your parcel will be returned to the sender.

(example — in real life this would link to a fake site; never actually click a button like this)

✅ Correct!

Correctly flagged as phishing. The signs you spotted:

  • The full email address isn’t PostNL’s: postnl-track-parcel.info
  • A tiny amount, designed to lower your guard
  • Time pressure (“within 24 hours”)
  • Delivery services never ask you to pay extra online via a link in an email

⚠️ That was wrong

This is a classic parcel-delivery scam. The signs you missed:

  • The full email address isn’t PostNL’s: postnl-track-parcel.info
  • A tiny amount, designed to lower your guard
  • Time pressure (“within 24 hours”)
  • Delivery services never ask you to pay extra online via a link in an email
From: ING Bank <security@ing-verify-online.com>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Important: your account will be blocked within 24 hours

Dear customer,

We have detected unusual activity on your account. To protect it, please re-verify your details within 24 hours. Failing to do so will result in your account being automatically blocked.

(example — in real life this would link to a fake site; never actually click a button like this)

✅ Correct!

Correctly flagged as phishing. The signs you spotted:

  • A bank always uses your real name, never “Dear customer”
  • The domain isn’t your bank’s real one, but ing-verify-online.com
  • Threatening a block within 24 hours creates pressure
  • Your bank never asks you to “verify” via a link in an email — always log in yourself via the app or a site you type in yourself

⚠️ That was wrong

This is a classic bank phishing email. The signs you missed:

  • A bank always uses your real name, never “Dear customer”
  • The domain isn’t your bank’s real one, but ing-verify-online.com
  • Threatening a block within 24 hours creates pressure
  • Your bank never asks you to “verify” via a link in an email — always log in yourself via the app or a site you type in yourself
From: Microsoft Account Team <account-security@microsoft-support-verify.net>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Unusual sign-in detected — action required

Hello,

We noticed a sign-in to your account from a new device. If this wasn’t you, secure your account within 1 hour, or access to your account will be revoked.

(example — in real life this would link to a fake site; never actually click a button like this)

✅ Correct!

Correctly flagged as phishing. The signs you spotted:

  • The domain isn’t microsoft.com but microsoft-support-verify.net
  • Extreme time pressure (“within 1 hour”) is a classic trick
  • A generic greeting (“Hello”) instead of your real name
  • Not sure? Log in yourself at account.microsoft.com (typed in yourself) to check your security — never via a link in an email

⚠️ That was wrong

This is a fake security alert. The signs you missed:

  • The domain isn’t microsoft.com but microsoft-support-verify.net
  • Extreme time pressure (“within 1 hour”) is a classic trick
  • A generic greeting (“Hello”) instead of your real name
  • Not sure? Log in yourself at account.microsoft.com (typed in yourself) to check your security — never via a link in an email
From: National Gift Promotion <winners@prize-payout-claim.com>
To: you@example.com
Subject: 🎉 Congratulations! You’ve won an iPhone 17 Pro

Congratulations!

You have been randomly selected as the winner of a free iPhone 17 Pro in our anniversary giveaway. To claim your prize, simply pay the shipping fee (€4.95) and enter your bank details for verification.

(example — in real life this would link to a fake site; never actually click a button like this)

✅ Correct!

Correctly flagged as phishing. The signs you spotted:

  • You never entered this “giveaway” — you can’t win something you never applied for
  • A genuine prize never asks you to pay first or enter your bank details
  • The domain prize-payout-claim.com sounds official but doesn’t really exist
  • “Too good to be true” usually is

⚠️ That was wrong

This is a classic prize scam. The signs you missed:

  • You never entered this “giveaway” — you can’t win something you never applied for
  • A genuine prize never asks you to pay first or enter your bank details
  • The domain prize-payout-claim.com sounds official but doesn’t really exist
  • “Too good to be true” usually is
From: Marieke de Vries <marieke.devries@companyname-inc.net>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Need something quick — just between us

Hi,

I’m in a meeting and can’t call. Could you quickly buy 4 gift cards of €50 for a client? Send me the codes as soon as you have them, I’ll pay you back once I can do my banking again. Keep this between us for now, I’ll explain later.

✅ Correct!

Correctly flagged as phishing. The signs you spotted:

  • Urgency + secrecy (“don’t mention this”, “keep this between us”) is a classic manipulation trick
  • An unusual request: buy gift cards and send the codes
  • “Can’t call” prevents you from double-checking
  • A colleague’s or manager’s real email almost never matches companyname-inc.net — always verify through another channel (phone, in person) before doing anything

⚠️ That was wrong

This is “CEO fraud”: someone impersonating a colleague or manager. The signs you missed:

  • Urgency + secrecy (“don’t mention this”, “keep this between us”) is a classic manipulation trick
  • An unusual request: buy gift cards and send the codes
  • “Can’t call” prevents you from double-checking
  • A colleague’s or manager’s real email almost never matches companyname-inc.net — always verify through another channel (phone, in person) before doing anything
From: Amazon <orders@amazon.com>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Your order #12345678 has shipped

Dear customer,

Good news: your order has shipped and is on its way. You can track its status via ‘Your Orders’ on amazon.com or in the Amazon app. Thanks for your order!

✅ Correct!

You correctly chose ‘safe’. The signs that confirm it:

  • The domain is genuinely correct: amazon.com
  • No urgency, no threats, no request to pay or enter details
  • Makes sense if you recently ordered something from Amazon
  • Still not sure? Log in to amazon.com separately (typed in yourself) to check your order, instead of clicking a link in the email

⚠️ That was wrong

You chose ‘safe’, but this was actually phishing. This email is actually genuinely safe — being cautious is fine, but this wasn’t phishing. The signs that it checks out:

  • The domain is genuinely correct: amazon.com
  • No urgency, no threats, no request to pay or enter details
  • Makes sense if you recently ordered something from Amazon
  • Still not sure? Log in to amazon.com separately (typed in yourself) to check your order, instead of clicking a link in the email

steps.title: Fake recruiters and 'too easy' side gigs
steps.body: A 'recruiter' who reaches out on LinkedIn, Instagram, or WhatsApp with too-good-to-be-true pay for too little work, and quickly asks for personal details or a 'deposit for equipment', is a scammer. Always check whether the company really exists and whether the recruiter has a verified profile with a shared connection.

lessons.title: Check whether your data has already been leaked

steps.title: Have I Been Pwned: check it yourself
steps.body: In virtually every major data breach (LinkedIn, Discord, various web shops), email addresses and sometimes passwords eventually end up on haveibeenpwned.com — the international standard for checking whether your data was included. Enter your email address and you'll immediately see which breaches you appear in.

steps.title: Check Je Hack from the Dutch police (optional)
steps.body: The Dutch police offer a similar, official check called Check Je Hack. Entirely optional alongside Have I Been Pwned, but a good second check from another official source.

steps.title: What it means if you show up
steps.body: Are you on one of these lists? Then there's a demonstrably higher chance of receiving targeted phishing and scam messages via email, text, WhatsApp, or DM — your address is marked as 'active' to criminals working with leaked lists. Respond by: changing the password of the leaked account right away, turning on 2FA wherever it isn't already, and staying extra critical of unexpected messages going forward.

steps.title: Ongoing monitoring
steps.body: Some password managers (like 1Password and Bitwarden) have built-in breach monitoring, which automatically warns you as soon as one of your saved accounts shows up in a new breach — more convenient than checking manually every time. We'll cover this further in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Password managers and 2FA: standard, not a luxury

steps.title: Why there's no getting around this anymore
steps.body: With dozens of accounts (school, work, social media, streaming, gaming), memorizing a unique, strong password for every site by hand just isn't realistic. A password manager (like Bitwarden, 1Password, or the one built into your browser/phone) is now standard gear — like a screen protector.

steps.title: Passkeys: the password's successor
steps.body: More and more services (Google, Apple, Instagram, banks) now support passkeys: logging in with your fingerprint or face, no password needed. More secure than a password, since there's nothing that can be stolen via a phishing email. Turn this on wherever you can.

steps.title: 2FA via an app, not SMS
steps.body: For 2FA, prefer an authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy) over SMS — SMS codes can be intercepted via 'SIM swapping' (your number gets taken over by a scammer, something that happens more often to young, active social-media users specifically).

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Check one of your most important accounts (email, bank, Instagram) to see whether app-based 2FA is set up, and turn it on if it isn't yet.

lessons.title: Recognizing identity theft and social engineering

steps.title: What is social engineering?
steps.body: Social engineering means manipulating people into giving up confidential information — often by putting you under pressure, creating urgency, or making you believe the sender has authority (your internship supervisor, the bank, the police) or is someone you trust.

steps.title: 'Hey, it's me! New number' — even among friends
steps.body: A message from a 'friend' or housemate with a new number, asking you to quickly transfer money because a payment 'isn't going through' — always verify this with a phone call to the known number or through another channel (like a shared group chat), never by replying directly to the new number.

steps.title: What to do if your identity is stolen
steps.body:
1. Change your passwords immediately, starting with your email
  2. Report it to your bank if financial details are involved
  3. File a police report
  4. Check MijnOverheid for unfamiliar entries under your name

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Think about it: would you immediately believe a message from a 'friend' with a new number and an urgent request for money, or check first through another channel?
